image_description: A male mallard duck (drake) floating on dark water. The duck features a glossy iridescent green head, a distinct white neck ring, a chestnut-brown breast, and a greyish-white body with black tail feathers. One orange webbed foot is visible paddling underwater. The background is dark, rippled water, and a concrete edge is visible in the bottom left corner.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The bill is clearly visible, broad, flat, and yellow-green in color, matching the description perfectly.
The eye is visible on the side of the head and appears dark/black, consistent with the taxonomy.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The body shape is robust and streamlined, sitting low in the water, indicating buoyancy and correct proportions.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image displays the classic Mallard drake pattern: iridescent green head, white neck ring, chestnut breast, and grey/white flanks.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: One orange leg/foot is visible underwater. While partially obscured by water refraction, the position (set back) and general webbed shape are consistent with anatomy.
The folded wing structure on the side of the body shows the correct layering of feathers and broad shape typical of waterfowl.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail is short, and the characteristic upward curl of the central black tail feathers (sexually dimorphic trait of Mallard drakes) is clearly visible.
